Oncology is the branch of medicine devoted entirely to cancer — its study, diagnosis, treatment, prevention, and the care of people living with it. A doctor who specialises in this field is called an oncologist.
What exactly is oncology concerned with?

Oncology is about understanding and fighting cancer. To grasp why this field exists as its own specialty, it helps to know what cancer is:

In a healthy body, cells grow, divide, and die in an orderly, controlled way. Cancer happens when something goes wrong in a cell's DNA, causing it to grow and divide uncontrollably. These rogue cells can pile up to form a mass called a tumour, invade nearby tissues, and even travel through the blood or lymphatic system to reach distant parts of the body — a process called metastasis.

Because cancer is so complex, unpredictable, and life-threatening, it demands its own entire field of medicine. That field is oncology.
What does an oncologist actually do?

An oncologist:

  • Diagnoses cancer by analysing test results, biopsies, scans, and blood work
  • Stages the cancer — meaning they figure out how advanced it is and whether it has spread
  • Plans and delivers treatment, which may include chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, hormone therapy, or a combination
  • Monitors the patient throughout and after treatment to check if the cancer is responding, returning, or spreading
  • Manages side effects of treatment, which can be harsh
  • Counsels patients and families about what to expect

Oncology is not a single, uniform field. It has several specialised sub-branches depending on the type of cancer, the organ involved, or the kind of treatment used:

By treatment method:

  • Medical oncology — uses drugs to treat cancer. This includes chemotherapy (drugs that kill fast-growing cells), targeted therapy (drugs that attack specific cancer cell features), immunotherapy (treatments that help your own immune system fight the cancer), and hormone therapy.
  • Surgical oncology — uses surgery to remove tumours and affected tissue.
  • Radiation oncology — uses high-energy radiation (like X-rays) to damage and kill cancer cells.

By the type of patient or organ:

  • Paediatric oncology — treats cancer specifically in children and adolescents, since childhood cancers differ significantly from those in adults.
  • Gynaecologic oncology — cancers of the female reproductive system (ovaries, uterus, cervix, etc.).
  • Haematologic oncology (haemato-oncology) — cancers of the blood and bone marrow, such as leukaemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma.
  • Neuro-oncology — cancers of the brain and spinal cord.
  • Thoracic oncology — cancers of the chest, including lung cancer.
  • Urologic oncology — cancers of the urinary and male reproductive systems (kidney, bladder, prostate, etc.).

Supportive and holistic branches:

  • Psycho-oncology — addresses the psychological and emotional impact of cancer on patients and their families.
  • Palliative oncology — focuses on improving quality of life, managing pain and symptoms, especially for patients in advanced stages where a cure may not be possible.

Oncology operates on two parallel tracks:

Clinical oncology is the practice of treating actual patients. Oncologists work in hospitals, cancer centres, and clinics.

Research oncology (also called oncology research or tumour biology) is the scientific investigation of how cancer forms, why it behaves the way it does, what makes certain people more vulnerable, and how new treatments can be developed. This is where cancer trials, lab experiments, and drug discovery happen.

Both are essential. Discoveries made in research oncology eventually become the treatments used in clinical oncology.
How is the word "oncology" used in everyday language?

• "She completed her residency in oncology." → She trained to become a cancer specialist.
  • "He was referred to the oncology department." → He was sent to the part of the hospital that handles cancer.
  • "Oncology has made remarkable advances in the last two decades." → The field of cancer medicine has improved greatly.
  • "Oncology nursing requires both technical skill and deep compassion." → Nursing in the context of cancer care.

When someone says "I have an oncology appointment," they mean an appointment with a cancer specialist.
One important distinction: benign vs. malignant tumours

Not every tumour is cancer. Oncology primarily deals with malignant tumours — tumours that grow aggressively, invade surrounding tissue, and can spread to other parts of the body. These are what we call cancer.

Benign tumours are non-cancerous. They grow slowly, stay in one place, and usually don't threaten life. Oncologists may still be involved in evaluating them (to confirm they are indeed benign), but they are not cancer.
Why oncology matters as its own field

Cancer is not one disease — it is hundreds of diseases. There are over 100 known types of cancer, each with its own behaviour, cause, and treatment approach. The biology is intricate, the treatments are powerful and often toxic, and the emotional weight on patients is immense. This complexity is precisely why oncology developed as a dedicated, deeply specialised branch of medicine, separate from general internal medicine or surgery.

In short: oncology = medicine's dedicated answer to cancer.
